nameStory: The 'dimorphic' jumping spider gets its scientific name from a fascinating quirk - its males come in two completely different forms that look so distinct they were once thought to be separate species! This extremely rare phenomenon in the animal world means you might see a black 'tufted' male with three fuzzy tufts on his head, or a striped 'gray' male with orange mouthparts, but they're actually the same species showing off different styles.
description: This medium-sized jumping spider is one of New England's most variable arachnids, especially among males. Females are typically brownish with subtle patterns, while males appear in two dramatically different forms - either jet black with distinctive hair tufts and pale legs, or boldly striped in black and white with bright orange pedipalps (the small appendages near their mouth). Like all jumping spiders, they have excellent vision with large, forward-facing eyes that give them an almost curious, intelligent expression. They're active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large, forward-facing eyes arranged in a square pattern dominate the face, with smaller eyes along the sides - these main eyes are remarkably sharp and will often seem to track your movement as you observe the spider

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build typical of jumping spiders with a relatively flat, rectangular front section (cephalothorax) and shorter, stockier legs compared to web-building spiders

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Males show extreme variation - either solid black with three prominent hair tufts on the head and cream-colored legs, or bold black and white stripes covering the entire body with orange palps

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky jumps rather than smooth walking, often pausing to orient toward movement or potential threats with their body facing you directly

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No capture web - instead creates small silk retreats or draglines, often found as tiny silk shelters in crevices of wooden structures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for a jumping spider, with females slightly larger and more robust than the males, easily fitting on a dime with legs extended

habitat: Commonly found on human-made structures like wooden fences, barn siding, decks, and outbuildings where they hunt for small insects. They favor sunny, vertical surfaces with cracks and crevices for shelter, particularly weathered wood that provides both hunting opportunities and hiding spots. While they can be found in natural settings, they show a strong preference for areas around homes and farms throughout New England's lowlands and foothills.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and become active as temperatures warm, with mating displays starting in late spring when both male forms can be observed performing their different courtship rituals.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen hunting on sunny surfaces during warm days, with females producing egg sacs in protected crevices.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, but activity decreases as temperatures drop and individuals seek overwintering sites in bark crevices or building gaps.
seasonality.winter: Inactive, overwintering as juveniles or adults in protected locations like under loose bark, in building crevices, or other insulated microsites.

funFact: The males' vision is actually sharper than a cat's and about 10 times better than a dragonfly's - they can spot and accurately judge the distance to a potential mate or prey from several body lengths away, making them some of the most visually acute hunters in the arthropod world!
confusionNotes: The two male forms are so different they were originally described as separate species, so don't second-guess yourself if you see dramatically different-looking males in the same area. The key is those unmistakable large forward-facing eyes and jumping behavior - no other New England spider has quite the same 'intelligent' stare and jerky movement pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This species beautifully demonstrates that nature doesn't always fit our tidy categories - the male dimorphism was so convincing that scientists initially classified them as different species until careful breeding studies in the 1950s proved they were the same. It's a reminder that even experts can be fooled by nature's variability.
compareHints: As the only Maevia species in New England, it's most likely to be confused with other jumping spiders in the family, but the extreme male dimorphism is unique. Other jumping spiders like the bold jumper or zebra spider may have variable patterns, but none show the dramatic either-or difference between solid black with tufts versus completely striped forms.
